oral.answer_heading: How battery capacity is measured:
oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."

oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. oral.answer_heading: Types of Heat Detectors:
oral.answer: 1. FIXED TEMPERATURE (bimetallic or fusible element type): Activates when ambient temperature rises ABOVE a fixed setpoint (typically 58°C, 68°C, or 88°C depending on location). Bimetallic strip deflects at setpoint temperature. Simple, low maintenance, but slow response for slowly developing fires. 2. RATE OF RISE (ROR): Activates when the RATE of temperature increase exceeds approximately 8–10°C per minute, regardless of actual temperature. Detects fast-developing fires earlier than fixed temperature type. Pneumatic ROR: Contains a small air chamber — rapid heating expands air faster than it can vent through a calibration port → diaphragm operates alarm contact. 3. COMBINED (Fixed Temp + ROR): Most common. Trips on EITHER: rate of rise > threshold OR fixed temperature exceeded — whichever comes first.

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 Hogging and Sagging
oral.answer: Hogging and sagging describe the longitudinal bending deformation of a ship's hull caused by the distribution of weight and buoyancy forces along the ship's length. These are fundamental structural concepts that an ETO must understand because excessive hogging or sagging leads to structural stress in the hull plating, frames, and girders, and in extreme cases can cause hull failure. Sagging occurs when the centre of the ship is supported by less buoyancy than its ends — the ship bends concave upward, like a hammock. This happens when: heavy cargo or ballast is concentrated amidships, the ship rides a wave trough amidships (wave crest at bow and stern), or the ship is loaded in port with heavy tanks at mid-length. oral.answer_heading: 11.2 Overspeed Trip — Principle and Testing
oral.answer: The overspeed trip is an independent safety device that shuts down the engine if speed exceeds 10–15% above rated RPM. It is completely independent of the governor and electronic control system — if the governor fails and allows the engine to accelerate uncontrolled, the overspeed trip provides the last line of defence against engine destruction. Connecting rods, crankshaft, and turbocharger impeller blades can fail at overspeed with catastrophic results.

oral.answer_heading: 8.1 Purifier Electrical Components and Starting
oral.answer: The centrifugal purifier (separator) operates at very high rotational speeds — typically 6,000 to 12,000 RPM depending on bowl size — to separate fuel or lube oil from water and sludge by centrifugal force. The high-speed rotating bowl represents a large stored kinetic energy and generates significant dynamic forces. Any imbalance at these speeds causes severe vibration that can damage the bowl, spindle bearings, and frame — potentially causing catastrophic bowl disintegration. The vibration trip is the primary protection against this.

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 Why Ships Corrode — The Electrochemical Cell
oral.answer: A ship's steel hull in seawater forms a natural electrochemical galvanic cell because seawater is an excellent electrolyte (salt concentration ~3.5%, conductivity ~50 mS/cm). Different areas of the hull surface have slightly different electrical potentials due to variations in steel grain structure, mill scale, weld joints, stress concentrations, and surface contamination. The more negative (active) area becomes the anode and corrodes, while the more positive (noble) area becomes the cathode and is protected. Without intervention, this causes accelerated corrosion at anodic areas, thinning the hull plating, pitting around welds, and degrading the propeller and rudder. The corrosion reaction at the anode is: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (iron dissolves into solution). At the cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ (oxygen reduction). oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?
oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Sanjib — where used on ships and why
oral.answer: Construction: Two rotor cages — outer cage (high resistance, low reactance) and inner cage (low resistance, high reactance). During starting: High frequency rotor currents flow mainly in outer cage (skin effect) → high resistance → high starting torque. Reduced inrush compared to full cage. During running: Low slip → low frequency → currents shift to inner cage → low resistance → efficient running, low losses. Used on ships for: windlass, mooring winch, anchor windlass, bow thruster auxiliary motors, cargo crane hoisting motors — all need HIGH STARTING TORQUE under load. Advantage over single cage: Better starting torque without requiring external resistance starter. Better PF at starting.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: Overload Relay vs Overcurrent Relay — Difference
oral.answer: Overload relay: Thermal bimetallic type. Protects motor from sustained overload (overcurrent < 10× FLA). Slow to trip — reflects thermal heating of motor winding. Overcurrent relay (OCR): IDMT type. Protects against fault currents and heavy short circuits. Fast trip proportional to current magnitude. Key difference: Overload = thermal protection (motor). OCR = fault protection (cables, busbar). Both may be present — different trip times. Fuse vs OCR: Fuse is sacrificial (single-use), trips on overcurrent, protects cables. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.

oral.answer_heading: 1.2 Two Methods of Cathodic Protection
oral.answer: Cathodic protection works by making the entire hull surface act as a cathode by supplying electrons externally, stopping the anodic dissolution reaction. There are two methods: sacrificial anode method (passive, galvanic) and impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP, active). Both methods force the hull potential to a negative value (typically –800 mV to –1050 mV relative to Ag/AgCl reference electrode) where steel corrosion effectively stops. The choice between methods depends on vessel size, dry dock interval, trade route, and maintenance capability.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib — 'Function of IGBT in cycloconverter'
oral.answer: Cycloconverter: Converts AC power directly to AC power at a DIFFERENT (lower) frequency — NO intermediate DC link. Limitation: Output frequency limited to <1/3 of input frequency. On 60Hz supply → max output 20Hz. On 50Hz → max 16.7Hz. Application: Large low-speed motors where low frequency needed (e.g. large propulsion drives, cement mills, rolling mills). IGBT in cycloconverter: IGBT (Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor) replaces SCR in modern designs. IGBT advantage: Gate-controlled turn-OFF (no natural commutation needed). Faster switching (2–20kHz vs 50–60Hz for SCR). Lower conduction losses. Better waveform quality. Dead ship context: After blackout, if cycloconverter-driven thruster — cannot start until ship's power restored fully.

oral.answer_heading: 5.1 Stray Current Corrosion Explained
oral.answer: Stray current corrosion is corrosion caused by electrical current flowing through an unintended path in the structure. In the context of a ship berthed at port with ICCP running, the impressed DC current can leak from the hull into the mooring lines (steel wire ropes or chains), the gangway, shore power cables, and through the seawater into the jetty steel piling. When this current exits any metallic component back into the seawater (completing the circuit), it causes accelerated corrosion at the exit point. The rate of stray current corrosion can be extremely rapid — 10 amps of stray DC current can dissolve approximately 10 kg of steel per year. Shore power connections are particularly problematic because the shore earth is connected to the ship's hull at the shore supply plug, effectively linking the ICCP circuit to the entire shore electrical earthing system. oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. oral.answer: How it works: (1) Press START (momentary) → coil K1 energises. (2) Aux contact K1-A (NO) closes in parallel with START button → seals in circuit. (3) Release START → K1-A keeps coil energised. (4) Press STOP (NC in series) → coil drops → K1-A opens → unlatched. Uses: Motor starters (stays running after start pressed). oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Main Components of ICCP System
oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential. The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. oral.answer: Definition: Motor runs stably at approximately 1/7th of synchronous speed instead of accelerating to full speed. Cause: 7th harmonic component in the air-gap flux creates a reluctance torque dip at 1/7 × Ns. Motor locks into this stable operating point instead of pulling through to full speed. Prevention: (1) Skew rotor slots — reduces harmonic content of air-gap flux. (2) Proper stator slot/rotor slot combination — avoid slot harmonics. (3) Chording of stator winding — reduces 5th and 7th harmonics. How to recognise: Motor starts, accelerates to ~1/7 speed, stops accelerating, runs noisily at low speed. Overcurrent relay may trip.

oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?

oral.answer: Cycloconverter: Converts AC power directly to AC power at a DIFFERENT (lower) frequency — NO intermediate DC link. Limitation: Output frequency limited to <1/3 of input frequency. On 60Hz supply → max output 20Hz. On 50Hz → max 16.7Hz. Application: Large low-speed motors where low frequency needed (e.g. large propulsion drives, cement mills, rolling mills). Faster switching (2–20kHz vs 50–60Hz for SCR). Lower conduction losses. Better waveform quality. Dead ship context: After blackout, if cycloconverter-driven thruster — cannot start until ship's power restored fully.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal, Sanjib — difference between fuse types
oral.answer: 1. Rewirable (Kit-Kat) fuse: Rating unknown (depends on wire gauge used). NOT safe for high fault current. Cheapest, least reliable. Replaced by inserting new wire element. 2. Cartridge fuse: Rating known (printed on body). NOT safe for high fault current. Reliable rating but may not clear high fault safely. 3. HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuse: MOST IMPORTANT. Rating stamped on end cap. Blows in 0.25–3 cycles. SAFE for high fault current. HRC internals: Ceramic or glass body, silver fuse element (calibrated cross-section), silica sand filler (quenches arc), riveted brass end caps. HRC advantage: Current limiting (arc extinguishes before current reaches peak), no arc flash, accurate and repeatable operation.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Sanjib — where used on ships and why
oral.answer: Construction: Two rotor cages — outer cage (high resistance, low reactance) and inner cage (low resistance, high reactance). During starting: High frequency rotor currents flow mainly in outer cage (skin effect) → high resistance → high starting torque. Reduced inrush compared to full cage. During running: Low slip → low frequency → currents shift to inner cage → low resistance → efficient running, low losses. Used on ships for: windlass, mooring winch, anchor windlass, bow thruster auxiliary motors, cargo crane hoisting motors — all need HIGH STARTING TORQUE under load. Advantage over single cage: Better starting torque without requiring external resistance starter. Better PF at starting.

oral.answer: Firing angle (α): The angle in the AC cycle at which the gate pulse is applied to turn the thyristor on. Effect: Lower α → thyristor conducts for longer period → higher average output voltage. α=0° → full output. α=180° → zero output. In a soft starter: Back-to-back SCRs per phase. At start: α=180° (zero voltage). Gradually decreased to 0° over starting period → voltage ramps up smoothly → torque ramps up → avoids inrush. Natural commutation: SCR turns OFF automatically when AC supply crosses zero — this is why SCR needs AC supply to turn off.

oral.answer_heading: 4.1 Why Poor Power Factor is Harmful
oral.answer: A low power factor has significant negative consequences for the ship's electrical system and must be corrected. When PF is low (e.g., 0.6 lagging), a larger current must be drawn from the generator to supply the same useful KW of power. This higher current causes: increased I²R losses (heating) in cables, transformers, and generator windings; reduced terminal voltage at the load end (increased voltage drop); generators reaching their KVA limit before their KW limit (the machine is full on current even though useful KW output is low); and increased fuel consumption by the prime mover to drive the generator at higher reactive current. Additionally, generators must be rated at a higher KVA for the same useful KW output. oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. On ships, the power factor is almost always lagging because the predominant loads are induction motors (pumps, fans, compressors, cargo winch

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib — 'Function of IGBT in cycloconverter'
oral.answer: Cycloconverter: Converts AC power directly to AC power at a DIFFERENT (lower) frequency — NO intermediate DC link. Limitation: Output frequency limited to <1/3 of input frequency. On 60Hz supply → max output 20Hz. On 50Hz → max 16.7Hz. Application: Large low-speed motors where low frequency needed (e.g. large propulsion drives, cement mills, rolling mills). IGBT in cycloconverter: IGBT (Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor) replaces SCR in modern designs. IGBT advantage: Gate-controlled turn-OFF (no natural commutation needed). Faster switching (2–20kHz vs 50–60Hz for SCR). Lower conduction losses. Better waveform quality. Dead ship context: After blackout, if cycloconverter-driven thruster — cannot start until ship's power restored fully.

oral.answer_heading: 4.1 Why Poor Power Factor is Harmful
oral.answer: A low power factor has significant negative consequences for the ship's electrical system and must be corrected. When PF is low (e.g., 0.6 lagging), a larger current must be drawn from the generator to supply the same useful KW of power. This higher current causes: increased I²R losses (heating) in cables, transformers, and generator windings; reduced terminal voltage at the load end (increased voltage drop); generators reaching their KVA limit before their KW limit (the machine is full on current even though useful KW output is low); and increased fuel consumption by the prime mover to drive the generator at higher reactive current. Additionally, generators must be rated at a higher KVA for the same useful KW output. oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. The idle machine runs as an induction motor (motoring effect) — draws current from busbar. Protection: Reverse power relay detects the reverse power flow and trips the ACB within seconds. If reverse power relay fails → overcurrent may develop. Why this matters: Closing ACB without synchronising (and without running) is a common exam trick — surveyor wants to hear 'motoring + reverse power trip'.

oral.answer_heading: How battery capacity is measured:
oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."

oral.text: IGBT in detail n its application
oral.answer_heading: Answer: NO — SCR cannot replace IGBT in the inverter stage of a VFD.
oral.answer: Why: SCR requires natural commutation — needs AC supply voltage to cross zero for turn-off. In the inverter stage the supply is DC — SCR cannot self-commutate in DC. It would stay ON permanently. SCR CAN be used in: Rectifier stage (AC→DC) of a VFD — used in regenerative/4-quadrant drives. But NOT the inverter stage (DC→AC). IGBT controls: Gate-controlled turn-on AND turn-off. Switched at 2–20kHz. Essential for PWM inverter. Modern VFD: Diode bridge rectifier + IGBT inverter (most common) OR SCR rectifier (regenerative) + IGBT inverter.

oral.answer: 1. Rewirable (Kit-Kat) fuse: Rating unknown (depends on wire gauge used). NOT safe for high fault current. Cheapest, least reliable. Replaced by inserting new wire element. 2. Cartridge fuse: Rating known (printed on body). NOT safe for high fault current. Reliable rating but may not clear high fault safely. 3. HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuse: MOST IMPORTANT. Rating stamped on end cap. Blows in 0.25–3 cycles. SAFE for high fault current. HRC internals: Ceramic or glass body, silver fuse element (calibrated cross-section), silica sand filler (quenches arc), riveted brass end caps. HRC advantage: Current limiting (arc extinguishes before current reaches peak), no arc flash, accurate and repeatable operation.

oral.answer_heading: Overload Relay vs Overcurrent Relay — Difference
oral.answer: Overload relay: Thermal bimetallic type. Protects motor from sustained overload (overcurrent < 10× FLA). Slow to trip — reflects thermal heating of motor winding. Overcurrent relay (OCR): IDMT type. Protects against fault currents and heavy short circuits. Fast trip proportional to current magnitude. Key difference: Overload = thermal protection (motor). OCR = fault protection (cables, busbar). Both may be present — different trip times. Fuse vs OCR: Fuse is sacrificial (single-use), trips on overcurrent, protects cables. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.

oral.text: How to measure cable insulation? Rating of cable? Will you measure or not? How to measure with megger?
oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib — 'Function of IGBT in cycloconverter'
oral.answer: Cycloconverter: Converts AC power directly to AC power at a DIFFERENT (lower) frequency — NO intermediate DC link. Limitation: Output frequency limited to <1/3 of input frequency. On 60Hz supply → max output 20Hz. On 50Hz → max 16.7Hz. Application: Large low-speed motors where low frequency needed (e.g. large propulsion drives, cement mills, rolling mills). IGBT in cycloconverter: IGBT (Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor) replaces SCR in modern designs. IGBT advantage: Gate-controlled turn-OFF (no natural commutation needed). Faster switching (2–20kHz vs 50–60Hz for SCR). Lower conduction losses. Better waveform quality. Dead ship context: After blackout, if cycloconverter-driven thruster — cannot start until ship's power restored fully.

oral.text: If Gate signal turned off, effect on thyristor
oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib, Gopikrishna — follow-up after thyristor explanation
oral.answer: Firing angle (α): The angle in the AC cycle at which the gate pulse is applied to turn the thyristor on. Effect: Lower α → thyristor conducts for longer period → higher average output voltage. α=0° → full output. α=180° → zero output. In a soft starter: Back-to-back SCRs per phase. At start: α=180° (zero voltage). Gradually decreased to 0° over starting period → voltage ramps up smoothly → torque ramps up → avoids inrush. Natural commutation: SCR turns OFF automatically when AC supply crosses zero — this is why SCR needs AC supply to turn off.

oral.answer: Definition: Motor runs stably at approximately 1/7th of synchronous speed instead of accelerating to full speed. Cause: 7th harmonic component in the air-gap flux creates a reluctance torque dip at 1/7 × Ns. Motor locks into this stable operating point instead of pulling through to full speed. Prevention: (1) Skew rotor slots — reduces harmonic content of air-gap flux. (2) Proper stator slot/rotor slot combination — avoid slot harmonics. (3) Chording of stator winding — reduces 5th and 7th harmonics. How to recognise: Motor starts, accelerates to ~1/7 speed, stops accelerating, runs noisily at low speed. Overcurrent relay may trip.

PN junction: P-type and N-type joined → depletion zone forms → built-in potential barrier (~0.7V silicon) Forward bias: overcomes barrier → current flows. oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib, Gopikrishna — follow-up after thyristor explanation
oral.answer: Firing angle (α): The angle in the AC cycle at which the gate pulse is applied to turn the thyristor on. Effect: Lower α → thyristor conducts for longer period → higher average output voltage. α=0° → full output. α=180° → zero output. In a soft starter: Back-to-back SCRs per phase. At start: α=180° (zero voltage). Gradually decreased to 0° over starting period → voltage ramps up smoothly → torque ramps up → avoids inrush. Natural commutation: SCR turns OFF automatically when AC supply crosses zero — this is why SCR needs AC supply to turn off.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Trick question — asked by multiple surveyors
oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. The idle machine runs as an induction motor (motoring effect) — draws current from busbar. Protection: Reverse power relay detects the reverse power flow and trips the ACB within seconds. If reverse power relay fails → overcurrent may develop. Why this matters: Closing ACB without synchronising (and without running) is a common exam trick — surveyor wants to hear 'motoring + reverse power trip'.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.text: Double cage induction motor and where used in ER
oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Sanjib — where used on ships and why
oral.answer: Construction: Two rotor cages — outer cage (high resistance, low reactance) and inner cage (low resistance, high reactance). During starting: High frequency rotor currents flow mainly in outer cage (skin effect) → high resistance → high starting torque. Reduced inrush compared to full cage. During running: Low slip → low frequency → currents shift to inner cage → low resistance → efficient running, low losses. Used on ships for: windlass, mooring winch, anchor windlass, bow thruster auxiliary motors, cargo crane hoisting motors — all need HIGH STARTING TORQUE under load. Advantage over single cage: Better starting torque without requiring external resistance starter. Better PF at starting.

oral.answer_heading: 2.2 GMDSS Battery — SOLAS Regulations
oral.answer: The GMDSS battery is a critical component — it must maintain all GMDSS equipment operational for the required duration without any other power source. SOLAS Chapter IV Regulation 13 specifies the battery requirements for GMDSS equipment. The battery must be of sufficient capacity to operate the radio installations for a minimum of 1 hour, or 6 hours for vessels making international voyages, after total loss of ship's main power and emergency power. The GMDSS battery is typically a sealed lead-acid battery or NiCd battery rated at 200 Ah (200 ampere-hours), designed to supply the GMDSS equipment at 24V DC. The battery is kept permanently on trickle charge from the ship's electrical supply (via a dedicated charger unit). oral.answer_heading: ER crane speed control methods:
oral.answer: 1. POLE CHANGING (Dahlander winding): 2-pole = high speed, 4-pole = low speed. Simple, two fixed speeds only. 2. ROTOR RESISTANCE (Slip ring motor): External resistance in rotor → increases slip → reduces speed. Steps depend on resistance steps. Good torque control for crane hoists. 3. VFD (Variable Frequency Drive): Full variable speed, smooth control, regenerative braking. Modern cranes.

oral.answer_heading: Types of Heat Detectors:
oral.answer: 1. FIXED TEMPERATURE (bimetallic or fusible element type): Activates when ambient temperature rises ABOVE a fixed setpoint (typically 58°C, 68°C, or 88°C depending on location). Bimetallic strip deflects at setpoint temperature. Simple, low maintenance, but slow response for slowly developing fires. 2. RATE OF RISE (ROR): Activates when the RATE of temperature increase exceeds approximately 8–10°C per minute, regardless of actual temperature. Detects fast-developing fires earlier than fixed temperature type. Pneumatic ROR: Contains a small air chamber — rapid heating expands air faster than it can vent through a calibration port → diaphragm operates alarm contact. 3. COMBINED (Fixed Temp + ROR): Most common. Trips on EITHER: rate of rise > threshold OR fixed temperature exceeded — whichever comes first.

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: 3.1 Megger — Construction and Working Principle
oral.answer: The megger (insulation resistance tester) is an instrument that applies a high DC voltage across the insulation under test and measures the very small leakage current that flows through it, displaying the ratio as resistance in Megohms (MΩ). The traditional hand-cranked (analogue) megger consists of three coils: the pressure coil (voltage coil), the deflecting coil (current coil), and the crossing coil — all mounted on a single spindle between the poles of a permanent magnet. The hand generator produces high DC voltage (500V, 1000V, or 2500V depending on the type). The deflection of the pointer depends on the ratio of currents in the two coils, which corresponds to the insulation resistance. Modern digital meggars are electronic instruments generating high DC voltage via a DC/DC converter, with digital display of resistance in MΩ or GΩ. oral.answer_heading: 2.1 What is GMDSS and Its Purpose
oral.answer: GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is an internationally agreed system using satellite and terrestrial radio communications to ensure that distress alerts and maritime safety information reach shore rescue co-ordination centres (RCCs) and nearby ships anywhere in the world. It is mandated by SOLAS Chapter IV for vessels on international voyages. GMDSS replaced the old Morse code distress system in 1999. The system is based on the concept of sea areas — the radio equipment required on a ship depends on which sea areas it operates in, because different equipment has different range capabilities. The four GMDSS sea areas are defined by the coverage of terrestrial VHF and MF/HF radio communications combined with satellite coverage. oral.answer_heading: What is a UV Flame Detector?

This makes it ideal for locations where a fire must be detected and suppressed before it spreads.

oral.answer_heading: Latching circuit: maintains energised state after the initiating signal is removed
oral.answer: How it works: (1) Press START (momentary) → coil K1 energises. (2) Aux contact K1-A (NO) closes in parallel with START button → seals in circuit. (3) Release START → K1-A keeps coil energised. (4) Press STOP (NC in series) → coil drops → K1-A opens → unlatched. Uses: Motor starters (stays running after start pressed). Alarm circuits (latches until reset). Fire/gas trips (must be manually reset). PLC implementation: SET coil (latch) and RESET coil — SET holds output ON, RESET cancels. Software equivalent of relay latching. Safety: Latching fire/gas alarm confirms condition occurred — cannot be cleared by momentary signal. Must acknowledge and manually reset.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Smoke Detectors
oral.answer: Smoke detectors are the most common fire detection devices onboard ship and are found in accommodation, machinery spaces, cargo holds, and control rooms. There are two principal types: ionisation smoke detectors and photoelectric (optical) smoke detectors. The ionisation smoke detector uses a tiny amount of radioactive material — Americium-241 (Am-241, alpha particle emitter) — to ionise the air between two charged electrodes inside a sensing chamber. When smoke particles enter the chamber, they attach to the ions, reducing the conductivity and therefore reducing the current. The electronics detect this drop in current and trigger the alarm. oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 What is GMDSS and Its Purpose
oral.answer: GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is an internationally agreed system using satellite and terrestrial radio communications to ensure that distress alerts and maritime safety information reach shore rescue co-ordination centres (RCCs) and nearby ships anywhere in the world. It is mandated by SOLAS Chapter IV for vessels on international voyages. GMDSS replaced the old Morse code distress system in 1999. The system is based on the concept of sea areas — the radio equipment required on a ship depends on which sea areas it operates in, because different equipment has different range capabilities. The four GMDSS sea areas are defined by the coverage of terrestrial VHF and MF/HF radio communications combined with satellite coverage. oral.answer_heading: What is WIDAS?
oral.answer: WIDAS = Water Ingress Detection and Alarm System. It is a monitoring system that detects the presence of water in enclosed spaces — cargo holds, void spaces, chain lockers, ballast tanks, fore and aft peaks — and raises an alarm on the bridge before flooding becomes structurally critical. WIDAS was introduced after a series of bulk carrier losses in the 1990s where water ingress in holds was not detected until too late.

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: Types of Heat Detectors:
oral.answer: 1. FIXED TEMPERATURE (bimetallic or fusible element type): Activates when ambient temperature rises ABOVE a fixed setpoint (typically 58°C, 68°C, or 88°C depending on location). Bimetallic strip deflects at setpoint temperature. Simple, low maintenance, but slow response for slowly developing fires. 2. RATE OF RISE (ROR): Activates when the RATE of temperature increase exceeds approximately 8–10°C per minute, regardless of actual temperature. Detects fast-developing fires earlier than fixed temperature type. Pneumatic ROR: Contains a small air chamber — rapid heating expands air faster than it can vent through a calibration port → diaphragm operates alarm contact. 3. COMBINED (Fixed Temp + ROR): Most common. Trips on EITHER: rate of rise > threshold OR fixed temperature exceeded — whichever comes first.

oral.answer_heading: What is a UV Flame Detector?
oral.answer: A UV (ultraviolet) flame detector is a fire detector that senses the ultraviolet radiation emitted by flames. This makes it ideal for locations where a fire must be detected and suppressed before it spreads.

oral.answer: Construction: Two rotor cages — outer cage (high resistance, low reactance) and inner cage (low resistance, high reactance). During starting: High frequency rotor currents flow mainly in outer cage (skin effect) → high resistance → high starting torque. Reduced inrush compared to full cage. During running: Low slip → low frequency → currents shift to inner cage → low resistance → efficient running, low losses. Used on ships for: windlass, mooring winch, anchor windlass, bow thruster auxiliary motors, cargo crane hoisting motors — all need HIGH STARTING TORQUE under load. Advantage over single cage: Better starting torque without requiring external resistance starter. Better PF at starting.

Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Purpose and Need for Viscosity Control
oral.answer: Heavy Fuel Oil (HFO) used in marine diesel engines must be heated before injection. The purpose of heating is to reduce viscosity to a level where the fuel can be properly atomised through the injector nozzle. Atomisation quality directly determines combustion efficiency, exhaust temperature, carbon deposit formation, and specific fuel consumption. Too high a viscosity means the fuel jet does not break into fine droplets — incomplete combustion follows. Too low a viscosity (over-heated) means reduced lubrication between the fuel pump plunger and barrel, accelerating wear and allowing fuel to blow past the plunger, causing injection timing errors. The correct injection viscosity is 10–14 cSt (centistokes) for most main engines, and 14–20 cSt for auxiliary diesel engines. oral.answer: The centrifugal purifier (separator) operates at very high rotational speeds — typically 6,000 to 12,000 RPM depending on bowl size — to separate fuel or lube oil from water and sludge by centrifugal force. The high-speed rotating bowl represents a large stored kinetic energy and generates significant dynamic forces. Any imbalance at these speeds causes severe vibration that can damage the bowl, spindle bearings, and frame — potentially causing catastrophic bowl disintegration. The vibration trip is the primary protection against this.

oral.answer_heading: Why temperature affects insulation resistance:
oral.answer: Insulation resistance is highly temperature-dependent — it DECREASES as temperature INCREASES (approximately halving for every 10°C rise). This means a motor that reads 10 MΩ at 80°C might read 160 MΩ if cooled to 40°C — both readings represent the same insulation. This is why IR values must ALWAYS be recorded with the temperature at time of test.

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?
oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. The current version is SOLAS 1974, as amended, which entered into force on 25 May 1980. It applies to all ships on international voyages. SOLAS sets out regulations covering structural safety, fire protection, life-saving appliances, radio communications, navigational safety, cargo management, nuclear ship safety, and high-speed craft. oral.answer_heading: 2.1 What is Droop and Why is it Necessary?
oral.answer: Droop is an intentional speed (or voltage) reduction characteristic built into generator control systems to enable stable parallel operation and automatic load sharing between generators. Without droop, two generators running in parallel with identical isochronous (flat, no-droop) governors would be unstable — if one generator picks up even a tiny amount of extra load, its governor would immediately increase fuel to restore speed, causing it to pick up even more load, eventually taking all the load and causing the other generator to motorise. Droop prevents this by making each generator's speed (and therefore frequency) decrease proportionally as its load increases — the generator with more load runs slightly slower, which automatically prevents it from taking further load. oral.answer: A marine cable is a multi-layer assembly, and the ETO must be able to name every layer from the innermost conductor outward. oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?
oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. oral.answer_heading: How battery capacity is measured:
oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, ALL — 'where does reactive power go?' — exact surveyor wording
oral.answer: Reactive power (kVAR) is NOT lost or dissipated as heat. It oscillates between the source and the load at twice the supply frequency. In an induction motor: kVAR sustains the rotating magnetic field that enables the rotor to develop torque. Without reactive power, no magnetic field, no torque. In a transformer: kVAR maintains core magnetisation (magnetising current). Core flux is sustained by reactive current. Returns to source every half cycle — travels back and forth between generator and load. Creates reactive current in cables, loading them without doing useful work (kW). This is why low PF increases cable/generator/transformer current for the same useful output — leading to overheating and losses. Answer in one sentence: 'Reactive power goes to the motor to sustain its magnetic field — it is returned to the source every half cycle, not consumed.'

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Sanjib — where used on ships and why
oral.answer: Construction: Two rotor cages — outer cage (high resistance, low reactance) and inner cage (low resistance, high reactance). During starting: High frequency rotor currents flow mainly in outer cage (skin effect) → high resistance → high starting torque. Reduced inrush compared to full cage. During running: Low slip → low frequency → currents shift to inner cage → low resistance → efficient running, low losses. Used on ships for: windlass, mooring winch, anchor windlass, bow thruster auxiliary motors, cargo crane hoisting motors — all need HIGH STARTING TORQUE under load. Advantage over single cage: Better starting torque without requiring external resistance starter. Better PF at starting.

oral.answer_heading: 4.1 Why Poor Power Factor is Harmful
oral.answer: A low power factor has significant negative consequences for the ship's electrical system and must be corrected. When PF is low (e.g., 0.6 lagging), a larger current must be drawn from the generator to supply the same useful KW of power. This higher current causes: increased I²R losses (heating) in cables, transformers, and generator windings; reduced terminal voltage at the load end (increased voltage drop); generators reaching their KVA limit before their KW limit (the machine is full on current even though useful KW output is low); and increased fuel consumption by the prime mover to drive the generator at higher reactive current. Additionally, generators must be rated at a higher KVA for the same useful KW output. oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Main Components of ICCP System
oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential. The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. The idle machine runs as an induction motor (motoring effect) — draws current from busbar. Protection: Reverse power relay detects the reverse power flow and trips the ACB within seconds. If reverse power relay fails → overcurrent may develop. Why this matters: Closing ACB without synchronising (and without running) is a common exam trick — surveyor wants to hear 'motoring + reverse power trip'.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Trick question — asked by multiple surveyors
oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. The idle machine runs as an induction motor (motoring effect) — draws current from busbar. Protection: Reverse power relay detects the reverse power flow and trips the ACB within seconds. If reverse power relay fails → overcurrent may develop. Why this matters: Closing ACB without synchronising (and without running) is a common exam trick — surveyor wants to hear 'motoring + reverse power trip'.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Main Components of ICCP System
oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential. The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. oral.answer: Rotating diode failure detection: stroboscope check during running — check for discoloured or pitted diodes. Also: unbalanced output voltage or ripple on output indicates a failed diode. Overvoltage protection on exciter output: Zener diode suppressor across diode bank — clamps transient voltages. Overcurrent protection on main field winding: included in AVR — limits excitation current to prevent winding overheating. Thermistor protection: embedded in stator winding — trips if temperature exceeds Class F limit (155°C). No slip rings — advantage: eliminates brush wear, arcing, and brush-dust contamination. Reduces maintenance significantly.

oral.text: While taking shore power if incoming frequency is low, your action?
oral.answer_heading: 1. If capacity is 80–100% of rated: ACCEPTABLE. Monitor more frequently.

oral.answer: Firing angle (α): The angle in the AC cycle at which the gate pulse is applied to turn the thyristor on. Effect: Lower α → thyristor conducts for longer period → higher average output voltage. α=0° → full output. α=180° → zero output. In a soft starter: Back-to-back SCRs per phase. At start: α=180° (zero voltage). Gradually decreased to 0° over starting period → voltage ramps up smoothly → torque ramps up → avoids inrush. Natural commutation: SCR turns OFF automatically when AC supply crosses zero — this is why SCR needs AC supply to turn off.

oral.answer_heading: Overload Relay vs Overcurrent Relay — Difference
oral.answer: Overload relay: Thermal bimetallic type. Protects motor from sustained overload (overcurrent < 10× FLA). Slow to trip — reflects thermal heating of motor winding. Overcurrent relay (OCR): IDMT type. Protects against fault currents and heavy short circuits. Fast trip proportional to current magnitude. Key difference: Overload = thermal protection (motor). OCR = fault protection (cables, busbar). Both may be present — different trip times. Fuse vs OCR: Fuse is sacrificial (single-use), trips on overcurrent, protects cables. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.

oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. oral.answer_heading: 3.1 Megger — Construction and Working Principle
oral.answer: The megger (insulation resistance tester) is an instrument that applies a high DC voltage across the insulation under test and measures the very small leakage current that flows through it, displaying the ratio as resistance in Megohms (MΩ). The traditional hand-cranked (analogue) megger consists of three coils: the pressure coil (voltage coil), the deflecting coil (current coil), and the crossing coil — all mounted on a single spindle between the poles of a permanent magnet. The hand generator produces high DC voltage (500V, 1000V, or 2500V depending on the type). The deflection of the pointer depends on the ratio of currents in the two coils, which corresponds to the insulation resistance. Modern digital meggars are electronic instruments generating high DC voltage via a DC/DC converter, with digital display of resistance in MΩ or GΩ. oral.answer_heading: How battery capacity is measured:
oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."

oral.answer_heading: 2.2 Reference Electrode — The Heart of ICCP
oral.answer: The reference electrode is the most critical sensing element in the ICCP system. It measures the electrochemical potential between the hull (cathode) and seawater, providing continuous feedback to the controller. Without an accurate reference electrode, the controller cannot determine whether the hull is under-protected (corrosion occurring) or over-protected (risk of hydrogen embrittlement and paint damage). The reference electrode must have a stable, predictable potential that does not change with temperature, salinity, or current flow — this is called a non-polarisable reference electrode. The Ag/AgCl (Silver/Silver Chloride) reference electrode is the most commonly used type because it is stable in seawater, has a well-defined potential of +0.222 V vs. Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), and has a long service life. oral.answer: Routine maintenance: Clean arc chutes (remove carbon deposits with dry cloth and compressed air). Check contact erosion — measure wear indicator. Lubricate operating mechanism (manufacturer-specified grease). Test trip coils (secondary injection). Check arc extinction plates alignment. Secondary injection test: Inject known AC current into relay secondary coil using test set. Increase until relay trips. Compare with IDMT curve. Tests relay WITHOUT passing real fault current — safe, repeatable. ACB isolation procedure: (1) Obtain PTW. (2) Open ACB — visually confirm open. (3) Rack out to isolated position. (4) Apply LOTO on racking handle. (5) Test for dead at ACB terminals BOTH sides. (6) Apply earth clamps to bus side. (7) Post 'Man Working' notice.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Main Components of ICCP System
oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential. The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. oral.answer: NON-RECHARGEABLE: Primary cell — chemical reaction is not easily reversible. Attempting to recharge can cause leakage, rupture, or fire. SPECIFIC GRAVITY: DOES NOT CHANGE during discharge. KOH concentration remains approximately constant. Hydrometer is USELESS for checking state of charge. State of charge check: Only method — measure open circuit voltage. Full: ~1.5V. Half: ~1.35V. Discharged: <1.1V. (Or conduct load test.) oral.answer_heading: Overload Relay vs Overcurrent Relay — Difference
oral.answer: Overload relay: Thermal bimetallic type. Protects motor from sustained overload (overcurrent < 10× FLA). Slow to trip — reflects thermal heating of motor winding. Overcurrent relay (OCR): IDMT type. Protects against fault currents and heavy short circuits. Fast trip proportional to current magnitude. Key difference: Overload = thermal protection (motor). OCR = fault protection (cables, busbar). Both may be present — different trip times. Fuse vs OCR: Fuse is sacrificial (single-use), trips on overcurrent, protects cables. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: Answer: NO — SCR cannot replace IGBT in the inverter stage of a VFD.
oral.answer: Why: SCR requires natural commutation — needs AC supply voltage to cross zero for turn-off. In the inverter stage the supply is DC — SCR cannot self-commutate in DC. IGBT controls: Gate-controlled turn-on AND turn-off. Switched at 2–20kHz. Essential for PWM inverter. Modern VFD: Diode bridge rectifier + IGBT inverter (most common) OR SCR rectifier (regenerative) + IGBT inverter.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib, Gopikrishna — follow-up after thyristor explanation
oral.answer: Firing angle (α): The angle in the AC cycle at which the gate pulse is applied to turn the thyristor on. Effect: Lower α → thyristor conducts for longer period → higher average output voltage. α=0° → full output. α=180° → zero output. In a soft starter: Back-to-back SCRs per phase. At start: α=180° (zero voltage). Gradually decreased to 0° over starting period → voltage ramps up smoothly → torque ramps up → avoids inrush. Natural commutation: SCR turns OFF automatically when AC supply crosses zero — this is why SCR needs AC supply to turn off.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Sanjib — where used on ships and why
oral.answer: Construction: Two rotor cages — outer cage (high resistance, low reactance) and inner cage (low resistance, high reactance). During starting: High frequency rotor currents flow mainly in outer cage (skin effect) → high resistance → high starting torque. Reduced inrush compared to full cage. During running: Low slip → low frequency → currents shift to inner cage → low resistance → efficient running, low losses. Used on ships for: windlass, mooring winch, anchor windlass, bow thruster auxiliary motors, cargo crane hoisting motors — all need HIGH STARTING TORQUE under load. Advantage over single cage: Better starting torque without requiring external resistance starter. Better PF at starting.

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: Overload Relay vs Overcurrent Relay — Difference
oral.answer: Overload relay: Thermal bimetallic type. Protects motor from sustained overload (overcurrent < 10× FLA). Slow to trip — reflects thermal heating of motor winding. Overcurrent relay (OCR): IDMT type. Protects against fault currents and heavy short circuits. Fast trip proportional to current magnitude. Key difference: Overload = thermal protection (motor). OCR = fault protection (cables, busbar). Both may be present — different trip times. Fuse vs OCR: Fuse is sacrificial (single-use), trips on overcurrent, protects cables. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.

oral.answer: The reference electrode is the most critical sensing element in the ICCP system. It measures the electrochemical potential between the hull (cathode) and seawater, providing continuous feedback to the controller. oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. oral.answer: Cycloconverter: Converts AC power directly to AC power at a DIFFERENT (lower) frequency — NO intermediate DC link. Limitation: Output frequency limited to <1/3 of input frequency. On 60Hz supply → max output 20Hz. On 50Hz → max 16.7Hz. Application: Large low-speed motors where low frequency needed (e.g. large propulsion drives, cement mills, rolling mills). IGBT in cycloconverter: IGBT (Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor) replaces SCR in modern designs. IGBT advantage: Gate-controlled turn-OFF (no natural commutation needed). Faster switching (2–20kHz vs 50–60Hz for SCR). Lower conduction losses. Better waveform quality. Dead ship context: After blackout, if cycloconverter-driven thruster — cannot start until ship's power restored fully.

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer: Overload relay: Thermal bimetallic type. Protects motor from sustained overload (overcurrent < 10× FLA). Slow to trip — reflects thermal heating of motor winding. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.

oral.answer_heading: 3.1 Megger — Construction and Working Principle
oral.answer: The megger (insulation resistance tester) is an instrument that applies a high DC voltage across the insulation under test and measures the very small leakage current that flows through it, displaying the ratio as resistance in Megohms (MΩ). The traditional hand-cranked (analogue) megger consists of three coils: the pressure coil (voltage coil), the deflecting coil (current coil), and the crossing coil — all mounted on a single spindle between the poles of a permanent magnet. The hand generator produces high DC voltage (500V, 1000V, or 2500V depending on the type). The deflection of the pointer depends on the ratio of currents in the two coils, which corresponds to the insulation resistance. Modern digital meggars are electronic instruments generating high DC voltage via a DC/DC converter, with digital display of resistance in MΩ or GΩ. The key reason a megger uses high DC voltage for IR

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: 2.2 Reference Electrode — The Heart of ICCP
oral.answer: The reference electrode is the most critical sensing element in the ICCP system. It measures the electrochemical potential between the hull (cathode) and seawater, providing continuous feedback to the controller. Without an accurate reference electrode, the controller cannot determine whether the hull is under-protected (corrosion occurring) or over-protected (risk of hydrogen embrittlement and paint damage). The reference electrode must have a stable, predictable potential that does not change with temperature, salinity, or current flow — this is called a non-polarisable reference electrode. The Ag/AgCl (Silver/Silver Chloride) reference electrode is the most commonly used type because it is stable in seawater, has a well-defined potential of +0.222 V vs. Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), and has a long service life. oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Main Components of ICCP System
oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential. The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. oral.answer_heading: Latching circuit: maintains energised state after the initiating signal is removed
oral.answer: How it works: (1) Press START (momentary) → coil K1 energises. (2) Aux contact K1-A (NO) closes in parallel with START button → seals in circuit. (3) Release START → K1-A keeps coil energised. (4) Press STOP (NC in series) → coil drops → K1-A opens → unlatched. Uses: Motor starters (stays running after start pressed). Alarm circuits (latches until reset). Fire/gas trips (must be manually reset). PLC implementation: SET coil (latch) and RESET coil — SET holds output ON, RESET cancels. Software equivalent of relay latching. Safety: Latching fire/gas alarm confirms condition occurred — cannot be cleared by momentary signal. Must acknowledge and manually reset.

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?
oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. On ships, the power factor is almost always lagging because the predominant loads are induction motors (pumps, fans, compressors, cargo winch

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib — 'Function of IGBT in cycloconverter'
oral.answer: Cycloconverter: Converts AC power directly to AC power at a DIFFERENT (lower) frequency — NO intermediate DC link. Limitation: Output frequency limited to <1/3 of input frequency. On 60Hz supply → max output 20Hz. On 50Hz → max 16.7Hz. Application: Large low-speed motors where low frequency needed (e.g. large propulsion drives, cement mills, rolling mills). IGBT in cycloconverter: IGBT (Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor) replaces SCR in modern designs. IGBT advantage: Gate-controlled turn-OFF (no natural commutation needed). Faster switching (2–20kHz vs 50–60Hz for SCR). Lower conduction losses. Better waveform quality. Dead ship context: After blackout, if cycloconverter-driven thruster — cannot start until ship's power restored fully.

oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, ALL surveyors
oral.answer: Routine maintenance: Clean arc chutes (remove carbon deposits with dry cloth and compressed air). Check contact erosion — measure wear indicator. Lubricate operating mechanism (manufacturer-specified grease). Test trip coils (secondary injection). Check arc extinction plates alignment. Secondary injection test: Inject known AC current into relay secondary coil using test set. Increase until relay trips. Compare with IDMT curve. Tests relay WITHOUT passing real fault current — safe, repeatable. ACB isolation procedure: (1) Obtain PTW. (2) Open ACB — visually confirm open. (3) Rack out to isolated position. oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kolkata surveyors, Sanjib — 'motor runs at slow speed after starting'
oral.answer: Definition: Motor runs stably at approximately 1/7th of synchronous speed instead of accelerating to full speed. Cause: 7th harmonic component in the air-gap flux creates a reluctance torque dip at 1/7 × Ns. Motor locks into this stable operating point instead of pulling through to full speed. Prevention: (1) Skew rotor slots — reduces harmonic content of air-gap flux. (2) Proper stator slot/rotor slot combination — avoid slot harmonics. (3) Chording of stator winding — reduces 5th and 7th harmonics. How to recognise: Motor starts, accelerates to ~1/7 speed, stops accelerating, runs noisily at low speed. Overcurrent relay may trip.

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.
