oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Main Components of ICCP System
oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential. The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. oral.answer_heading: 2.2 Reference Electrode — The Heart of ICCP
oral.answer: The reference electrode is the most critical sensing element in the ICCP system. It measures the electrochemical potential between the hull (cathode) and seawater, providing continuous feedback to the controller. Without an accurate reference electrode, the controller cannot determine whether the hull is under-protected (corrosion occurring) or over-protected (risk of hydrogen embrittlement and paint damage). The reference electrode must have a stable, predictable potential that does not change with temperature, salinity, or current flow — this is called a non-polarisable reference electrode. oral.answer_heading: Latching circuit: maintains energised state after the initiating signal is removed
oral.answer: How it works: (1) Press START (momentary) → coil K1 energises. (2) Aux contact K1-A (NO) closes in parallel with START button → seals in circuit. (3) Release START → K1-A keeps coil energised. (4) Press STOP (NC in series) → coil drops → K1-A opens → unlatched. Uses: Motor starters (stays running after start pressed). Alarm circuits (latches until reset). Fire/gas trips (must be manually reset). PLC implementation: SET coil (latch) and RESET coil — SET holds output ON, RESET cancels. oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. oral.answer_heading: Turbocharger RPM Sensor — Type and Working
oral.answer: Type: Magnetic pickup (variable reluctance) sensor — most common. Some high-speed TCs use eddy current or optical sensors. Working: Ferromagnetic toothed wheel (phonic wheel) on TC shaft rotates past sensor tip. Each tooth passing changes magnetic flux through sensor coil — induces voltage pulse. Frequency of pulses = RPM of TC. Calibration: Count teeth × pulses per tooth × conversion factor = RPM. Usually preconfigured in tachometer. Faults: Oil on sensor tip → weak signal. Air gap too large (>2mm) → no signal. Broken tooth → erratic RPM. Cable fault → zero reading. Clean tip, check gap during maintenance.

oral.answer_heading: Advantages of NiCd over lead-acid:
oral.answer: 1. TEMPERATURE PERFORMANCE: NiCd retains capacity at low temperatures (-20°C) far better than lead-acid. Essential for lifeboats in cold climates — lifeboat batteries on all ships are often NiCd. 2. CYCLE LIFE: 1,000–2,000 charge/discharge cycles (lead-acid: 300–500 cycles). Much longer service life. 3. STORAGE IN DISCHARGED STATE: NiCd can be stored fully discharged without damage — just recharge when needed. Lead-acid stored discharged → sulphation → permanent capacity loss. 4. OVERCHARGE TOLERANCE: NiCd handles overcharging better than lead-acid — internal chemistry accommodates slight overcharge.

oral.answer_heading: Answer: NO — SCR cannot replace IGBT in the inverter stage of a VFD.
oral.answer: Why: SCR requires natural commutation — needs AC supply voltage to cross zero for turn-off. In the inverter stage the supply is DC — SCR cannot self-commutate in DC. It would stay ON permanently. SCR CAN be used in: Rectifier stage (AC→DC) of a VFD — used in regenerative/4-quadrant drives. But NOT the inverter stage (DC→AC). IGBT controls: Gate-controlled turn-on AND turn-off. Switched at 2–20kHz. Essential for PWM inverter. Modern VFD: Diode bridge rectifier + IGBT inverter (most common) OR SCR rectifier (regenerative) + IGBT inverter.

oral.answer_heading: 1.2 Two Methods of Cathodic Protection
oral.answer: Cathodic protection works by making the entire hull surface act as a cathode by supplying electrons externally, stopping the anodic dissolution reaction. There are two methods: sacrificial anode method (passive, galvanic) and impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP, active). Both methods force the hull potential to a negative value (typically –800 mV to –1050 mV relative to Ag/AgCl reference electrode) where steel corrosion effectively stops. The choice between methods depends on vessel size, dry dock interval, trade route, and maintenance capability.

oral.answer: Cycloconverter: Converts AC power directly to AC power at a DIFFERENT (lower) frequency — NO intermediate DC link. Limitation: Output frequency limited to <1/3 of input frequency. On 60Hz supply → max output 20Hz. On 50Hz → max 16.7Hz. Application: Large low-speed motors where low frequency needed (e.g. large propulsion drives, cement mills, rolling mills). IGBT in cycloconverter: IGBT (Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor) replaces SCR in modern designs. IGBT advantage: Gate-controlled turn-OFF (no natural commutation needed). Faster switching (2–20kHz vs 50–60Hz for SCR). Lower conduction losses. Better waveform quality. Dead ship context: After blackout, if cycloconverter-driven thruster — cannot start until ship's power restored fully.

oral.answer_heading: 3.1 Megger — Construction and Working Principle
oral.answer: The megger (insulation resistance tester) is an instrument that applies a high DC voltage across the insulation under test and measures the very small leakage current that flows through it, displaying the ratio as resistance in Megohms (MΩ). The traditional hand-cranked (analogue) megger consists of three coils: the pressure coil (voltage coil), the deflecting coil (current coil), and the crossing coil — all mounted on a single spindle between the poles of a permanent magnet. The hand generator produces high DC voltage (500V, 1000V, or 2500V depending on the type). The deflection of the pointer depends on the ratio of currents in the two coils, which corresponds to the insulation resistance. Modern digital meggars are electronic instruments generating high DC voltage via a DC/DC converter, with digital display of resistance in MΩ or GΩ. oral.answer_heading: How battery capacity is measured:
oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."

oral.answer_heading: Turbocharger RPM Sensor — Type and Working
oral.answer: Type: Magnetic pickup (variable reluctance) sensor — most common. Some high-speed TCs use eddy current or optical sensors. Working: Ferromagnetic toothed wheel (phonic wheel) on TC shaft rotates past sensor tip. Each tooth passing changes magnetic flux through sensor coil — induces voltage pulse. Frequency of pulses = RPM of TC. Calibration: Count teeth × pulses per tooth × conversion factor = RPM. Usually preconfigured in tachometer. Faults: Oil on sensor tip → weak signal. Air gap too large (>2mm) → no signal. Broken tooth → erratic RPM. Cable fault → zero reading. Clean tip, check gap during maintenance.

oral.answer: Why: SCR requires natural commutation — needs AC supply voltage to cross zero for turn-off. In the inverter stage the supply is DC — SCR cannot self-commutate in DC. IGBT controls: Gate-controlled turn-on AND turn-off. Switched at 2–20kHz. Essential for PWM inverter. Modern VFD: Diode bridge rectifier + IGBT inverter (most common) OR SCR rectifier (regenerative) + IGBT inverter.

oral.answer_heading: How battery capacity is measured:
oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Main Components of ICCP System
oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential. The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?
oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. oral.answer: 1. Rewirable (Kit-Kat) fuse: Rating unknown (depends on wire gauge used). NOT safe for high fault current. Cheapest, least reliable. Replaced by inserting new wire element. 2. Cartridge fuse: Rating known (printed on body). NOT safe for high fault current. Reliable rating but may not clear high fault safely. 3. HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuse: MOST IMPORTANT. Rating stamped on end cap. Blows in 0.25–3 cycles. SAFE for high fault current. HRC internals: Ceramic or glass body, silver fuse element (calibrated cross-section), silica sand filler (quenches arc), riveted brass end caps. HRC advantage: Current limiting (arc extinguishes before current reaches peak), no arc flash, accurate and repeatable operation.

oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. The idle machine runs as an induction motor (motoring effect) — draws current from busbar. Protection: Reverse power relay detects the reverse power flow and trips the ACB within seconds. If reverse power relay fails → overcurrent may develop. oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Asked by ALL surveyors — most common switchboard question
oral.answer: 1. Dead-front panel construction: Cannot open live panel door — physical/electrical interlock prevents access to live conductors. 2. IDMT Over-current relay (OCR): Inverse Definite Minimum Time — trips FASTER for higher fault current. Protects busbars and feeders. 3. Under-voltage (UV) trip relay: Trips generator ACB if voltage drops below ~85% rated. Prevents motoring. 4. Reverse power relay: Detects power flow FROM busbar INTO generator — trips ACB. Prevents motoring of alternator. 5. Earth fault indicator lamps: Three lamps in star configuration. Normal = all glow equally. Fault = earthed phase lamp goes dim/dark. 6. Bus-tie (BT) interlock: Prevents wrong buses being paralleled. Ensures only correctly synchronised sections connected. 7. Preferential trip relay: Sheds non-essential loads sequentially (in stages) to prevent overload and blackout.

oral.answer_heading: 4.1 Why Poor Power Factor is Harmful
oral.answer: A low power factor has significant negative consequences for the ship's electrical system and must be corrected. When PF is low (e.g., 0.6 lagging), a larger current must be drawn from the generator to supply the same useful KW of power. This higher current causes: increased I²R losses (heating) in cables, transformers, and generator windings; reduced terminal voltage at the load end (increased voltage drop); generators reaching their KVA limit before their KW limit (the machine is full on current even though useful KW output is low); and increased fuel consumption by the prime mover to drive the generator at higher reactive current. Additionally, generators must be rated at a higher KVA for the same useful KW output. oral.answer_heading: Overload Relay vs Overcurrent Relay — Difference
oral.answer: Overload relay: Thermal bimetallic type. Protects motor from sustained overload (overcurrent < 10× FLA). Slow to trip — reflects thermal heating of motor winding. Overcurrent relay (OCR): IDMT type. Protects against fault currents and heavy short circuits. Fast trip proportional to current magnitude. Key difference: Overload = thermal protection (motor). OCR = fault protection (cables, busbar). Both may be present — different trip times. Fuse vs OCR: Fuse is sacrificial (single-use), trips on overcurrent, protects cables. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.

oral.answer: Rotating diode failure detection: stroboscope check during running — check for discoloured or pitted diodes. Also: unbalanced output voltage or ripple on output indicates a failed diode. oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Trick question — asked by multiple surveyors
oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. The idle machine runs as an induction motor (motoring effect) — draws current from busbar. Protection: Reverse power relay detects the reverse power flow and trips the ACB within seconds. If reverse power relay fails → overcurrent may develop. Why this matters: Closing ACB without synchronising (and without running) is a common exam trick — surveyor wants to hear 'motoring + reverse power trip'.

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 Electrical Specification of Tankers — Key Differences
oral.answer: Tankers carry flammable liquid cargo (crude oil, petroleum products, LPG, LNG, chemicals) which produce flammable vapours. This makes the electrical safety requirements on tankers fundamentally different from cargo ships. The hazardous areas on a tanker — pump rooms, cargo tank decks, cofferdams, void spaces, and any areas where flammable vapour may accumulate — require all electrical equipment to be of explosion-protected (Ex-rated) construction to prevent ignition of the surrounding atmosphere. Tanker electrical systems typically operate at 440V LV for domestic services and 6.6 kV HV for large cargo pump motors on crude oil tankers. The earthing system is insulated neutral (IT system) as on all ships — first earth fault does not trip supply. oral.answer: GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is an internationally agreed system using satellite and terrestrial radio communications to ensure that distress alerts and maritime safety information reach shore rescue co-ordination centres (RCCs) and nearby ships anywhere in the world. The system is based on the concept of sea areas — the radio equipment required on a ship depends on which sea areas it operates in, because different equipment has different range capabilities. The four GMDSS sea areas are defined by the coverage of terrestrial VHF and MF/HF radio communications combined with satellite coverage. oral.answer: The centrifugal purifier (separator) operates at very high rotational speeds — typically 6,000 to 12,000 RPM depending on bowl size — to separate fuel or lube oil from water and sludge by centrifugal force. oral.answer: The SART (Search and Rescue Radar Transponder) is a survival craft locating device that operates at 9 GHz — the same frequency as X-band RADAR. It is a passive device carried on survival craft (lifeboats, liferafts) that remains silent until it receives a 9 GHz RADAR pulse from a searching vessel or aircraft. When triggered, it responds by transmitting a series of 12 pulses on the same frequency, creating a distinctive 12-dot line pattern on the searching vessel's X-band RADAR PPI display, extending radially from the SART's position. The SART can respond to a ship's RADAR at a range of approximately 5 nautical miles and to an aircraft's RADAR at approximately 10 nautical miles. The SART also has a visual indicator (flashing LED) and audible alarm to alert survivors when it is being interrogated by a RADAR — this confirms that a ship or aircraft is searching and approaching. oral.answer_heading: Types of Heat Detectors:
oral.answer: 1. FIXED TEMPERATURE (bimetallic or fusible element type): Activates when ambient temperature rises ABOVE a fixed setpoint (typically 58°C, 68°C, or 88°C depending on location). Bimetallic strip deflects at setpoint temperature. Simple, low maintenance, but slow response for slowly developing fires. 2. RATE OF RISE (ROR): Activates when the RATE of temperature increase exceeds approximately 8–10°C per minute, regardless of actual temperature. Detects fast-developing fires earlier than fixed temperature type. Pneumatic ROR: Contains a small air chamber — rapid heating expands air faster than it can vent through a calibration port → diaphragm operates alarm contact. 3. COMBINED (Fixed Temp + ROR): Most common. Trips on EITHER: rate of rise > threshold OR fixed temperature exceeded — whichever comes first.

oral.answer_heading: 1.2 Two Methods of Cathodic Protection
oral.answer: Cathodic protection works by making the entire hull surface act as a cathode by supplying electrons externally, stopping the anodic dissolution reaction. There are two methods: sacrificial anode method (passive, galvanic) and impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP, active). Both methods force the hull potential to a negative value (typically –800 mV to –1050 mV relative to Ag/AgCl reference electrode) where steel corrosion effectively stops. The choice between methods depends on vessel size, dry dock interval, trade route, and maintenance capability.

oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. oral.answer_heading: 2.2 Reference Electrode — The Heart of ICCP
oral.answer: The reference electrode is the most critical sensing element in the ICCP system. It measures the electrochemical potential between the hull (cathode) and seawater, providing continuous feedback to the controller. Without an accurate reference electrode, the controller cannot determine whether the hull is under-protected (corrosion occurring) or over-protected (risk of hydrogen embrittlement and paint damage). The reference electrode must have a stable, predictable potential that does not change with temperature, salinity, or current flow — this is called a non-polarisable reference electrode. The Ag/AgCl (Silver/Silver Chloride) reference electrode is the most commonly used type because it is stable in seawater, has a well-defined potential of +0.222 V vs. Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), and has a long service life. oral.answer_heading: Types of Heat Detectors:
oral.answer: 1. FIXED TEMPERATURE (bimetallic or fusible element type): Activates when ambient temperature rises ABOVE a fixed setpoint (typically 58°C, 68°C, or 88°C depending on location). Bimetallic strip deflects at setpoint temperature. Simple, low maintenance, but slow response for slowly developing fires. 2. RATE OF RISE (ROR): Activates when the RATE of temperature increase exceeds approximately 8–10°C per minute, regardless of actual temperature. Detects fast-developing fires earlier than fixed temperature type. Pneumatic ROR: Contains a small air chamber — rapid heating expands air faster than it can vent through a calibration port → diaphragm operates alarm contact. 3. COMBINED (Fixed Temp + ROR): Most common. Trips on EITHER: rate of rise > threshold OR fixed temperature exceeded — whichever comes first.

oral.answer_heading: 5.1 Stray Current Corrosion Explained
oral.answer: Stray current corrosion is corrosion caused by electrical current flowing through an unintended path in the structure. In the context of a ship berthed at port with ICCP running, the impressed DC current can leak from the hull into the mooring lines (steel wire ropes or chains), the gangway, shore power cables, and through the seawater into the jetty steel piling. When this current exits any metallic component back into the seawater (completing the circuit), it causes accelerated corrosion at the exit point. The rate of stray current corrosion can be extremely rapid — 10 amps of stray DC current can dissolve approximately 10 kg of steel per year. Shore power connections are particularly problematic because the shore earth is connected to the ship's hull at the shore supply plug, effectively linking the ICCP circuit to the entire shore electrical earthing system. This creates unpredictabl

oral.answer_heading: Turbocharger RPM Sensor — Type and Working
oral.answer: Type: Magnetic pickup (variable reluctance) sensor — most common. Some high-speed TCs use eddy current or optical sensors. Working: Ferromagnetic toothed wheel (phonic wheel) on TC shaft rotates past sensor tip. Each tooth passing changes magnetic flux through sensor coil — induces voltage pulse. Frequency of pulses = RPM of TC. Calibration: Count teeth × pulses per tooth × conversion factor = RPM. Usually preconfigured in tachometer. Faults: Oil on sensor tip → weak signal. Air gap too large (>2mm) → no signal. Broken tooth → erratic RPM. Cable fault → zero reading. Clean tip, check gap during maintenance.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer: BITT = Built-In Integrity Test: Automatic self-test function built into the navigation light control panel. What it tests: Lamp filament continuity, supply fuse status, supply voltage level, cable continuity to each light fitting. How: Controller briefly energises each circuit and measures current — if current = 0 or below threshold → lamp/fuse fault → alarm generated. Alarm output: Audible + visual alarm on bridge panel. ETO action on BITT alarm: Check lamp at fitting location. Replace lamp. Reset alarm. Test BITT — confirm clear.

oral.answer: Rotating diode failure detection: stroboscope check during running — check for discoloured or pitted diodes. Also: unbalanced output voltage or ripple on output indicates a failed diode. Reduces maintenance significantly.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib, Gopikrishna — follow-up after thyristor explanation
oral.answer: Firing angle (α): The angle in the AC cycle at which the gate pulse is applied to turn the thyristor on. Effect: Lower α → thyristor conducts for longer period → higher average output voltage. α=0° → full output. α=180° → zero output. In a soft starter: Back-to-back SCRs per phase. At start: α=180° (zero voltage). Gradually decreased to 0° over starting period → voltage ramps up smoothly → torque ramps up → avoids inrush. Natural commutation: SCR turns OFF automatically when AC supply crosses zero — this is why SCR needs AC supply to turn off.

oral.answer: Tankers carry flammable liquid cargo (crude oil, petroleum products, LPG, LNG, chemicals) which produce flammable vapours. This makes the electrical safety requirements on tankers fundamentally different from cargo ships. The hazardous areas on a tanker — pump rooms, cargo tank decks, cofferdams, void spaces, and any areas where flammable vapour may accumulate — require all electrical equipment to be of explosion-protected (Ex-rated) construction to prevent ignition of the surrounding atmosphere. Tanker electrical systems typically operate at 440V LV for domestic services and 6.6 kV HV for large cargo pump motors on crude oil tankers. The earthing system is insulated neutral (IT system) as on all ships — first earth fault does not trip supply. oral.answer_heading: 1.1 Hogging and Sagging
oral.answer: Hogging and sagging describe the longitudinal bending deformation of a ship's hull caused by the distribution of weight and buoyancy forces along the ship's length. These are fundamental structural concepts that an ETO must understand because excessive hogging or sagging leads to structural stress in the hull plating, frames, and girders, and in extreme cases can cause hull failure. Sagging occurs when the centre of the ship is supported by less buoyancy than its ends — the ship bends concave upward, like a hammock. This happens when: heavy cargo or ballast is concentrated amidships, the ship rides a wave trough amidships (wave crest at bow and stern), or the ship is loaded in port with heavy tanks at mid-length. oral.answer_heading: 1.1 Cable Construction — Layers from Inside Out
oral.answer: A marine cable is a multi-layer assembly, and the ETO must be able to name every layer from the innermost conductor outward. The layers serve distinct functions: electrical conduction, insulation, filling/bedding, mechanical protection, and outer sheathing. Understanding each layer is necessary both for correct cable selection and for answering the examiner's question about 'all layers in a cable.' The standard shipboard power cable construction from inside to outside is: Conductor → Conductor Screen (HV only) → Insulation → Insulation Screen (HV only) → Metallic Screen/Tape (HV only) → Bedding/Inner Sheath → Armour → Outer Sheath. The conductor is typically stranded copper (flexible, low resistance), though aluminium conductors are used in shore installations but rarely on ships due to corrosion concerns. oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: Mooring Winch Autotension — Working and ETO Maintenance
oral.answer: Working: Motor drives drum. Load cell or current sensing detects rope tension. When tension > setpoint → motor reverses/brakes → pays out rope. When tension < setpoint → motor hauls in. Maintains constant tension automatically during tidal/current changes. ETO maintenance: Check motor IR, check brake condition (air gap of electromagnetic brake), check limit switches (inboard/outboard), check hydraulic pressure if hydraulic drive type, verify load cell calibration. Autotension interlock: Must be manually cancelled before departure — if left in auto, winch will keep paying out rope as ship moves away.

oral.answer_heading: 2.2 Reference Electrode — The Heart of ICCP
oral.answer: The reference electrode is the most critical sensing element in the ICCP system. It measures the electrochemical potential between the hull (cathode) and seawater, providing continuous feedback to the controller. Without an accurate reference electrode, the controller cannot determine whether the hull is under-protected (corrosion occurring) or over-protected (risk of hydrogen embrittlement and paint damage). The reference electrode must have a stable, predictable potential that does not change with temperature, salinity, or current flow — this is called a non-polarisable reference electrode. The Ag/AgCl (Silver/Silver Chloride) reference electrode is the most commonly used type because it is stable in seawater, has a well-defined potential of +0.222 V vs. Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), and has a long service life. oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Trick question — asked by multiple surveyors
oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. The idle machine runs as an induction motor (motoring effect) — draws current from busbar. Protection: Reverse power relay detects the reverse power flow and trips the ACB within seconds. If reverse power relay fails → overcurrent may develop. Why this matters: Closing ACB without synchronising (and without running) is a common exam trick — surveyor wants to hear 'motoring + reverse power trip'.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal, Sanjib — difference between fuse types
oral.answer: 1. Rewirable (Kit-Kat) fuse: Rating unknown (depends on wire gauge used). NOT safe for high fault current. Cheapest, least reliable. Replaced by inserting new wire element. 2. Cartridge fuse: Rating known (printed on body). NOT safe for high fault current. Reliable rating but may not clear high fault safely. 3. HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuse: MOST IMPORTANT. Rating stamped on end cap. Blows in 0.25–3 cycles. SAFE for high fault current. HRC internals: Ceramic or glass body, silver fuse element (calibrated cross-section), silica sand filler (quenches arc), riveted brass end caps. HRC advantage: Current limiting (arc extinguishes before current reaches peak), no arc flash, accurate and repeatable operation.

oral.answer_heading: What is ODP?
oral.answer: ODP = Ozone Depletion Potential. A dimensionless number that describes the relative amount of damage a substance can cause to the stratospheric ozone layer, compared to CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) which has a reference ODP of 1.0. The higher the ODP, the more damaging the substance is to the ozone layer that protects the Earth from harmful UV-B radiation.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Sanjib — where used on ships and why
oral.answer: Construction: Two rotor cages — outer cage (high resistance, low reactance) and inner cage (low resistance, high reactance). During starting: High frequency rotor currents flow mainly in outer cage (skin effect) → high resistance → high starting torque. Reduced inrush compared to full cage. During running: Low slip → low frequency → currents shift to inner cage → low resistance → efficient running, low losses. Used on ships for: windlass, mooring winch, anchor windlass, bow thruster auxiliary motors, cargo crane hoisting motors — all need HIGH STARTING TORQUE under load. Advantage over single cage: Better starting torque without requiring external resistance starter. Better PF at starting.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Asked by ALL surveyors — most common switchboard question
oral.answer: 1. Dead-front panel construction: Cannot open live panel door — physical/electrical interlock prevents access to live conductors. 2. IDMT Over-current relay (OCR): Inverse Definite Minimum Time — trips FASTER for higher fault current. Protects busbars and feeders. 3. Under-voltage (UV) trip relay: Trips generator ACB if voltage drops below ~85% rated. Prevents motoring. 4. Reverse power relay: Detects power flow FROM busbar INTO generator — trips ACB. Prevents motoring of alternator. 5. Earth fault indicator lamps: Three lamps in star configuration. Normal = all glow equally. Fault = earthed phase lamp goes dim/dark. 6. Bus-tie (BT) interlock: Prevents wrong buses being paralleled. Ensures only correctly synchronised sections connected. 7. Preferential trip relay: Sheds non-essential loads sequentially (in stages) to prevent overload and blackout.

oral.answer_heading: How battery capacity is measured:
oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."

oral.text: Exd and exi where used on chemical tankers
oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: Mooring Winch Autotension — Working and ETO Maintenance
oral.answer: Working: Motor drives drum. Load cell or current sensing detects rope tension. When tension > setpoint → motor reverses/brakes → pays out rope. When tension < setpoint → motor hauls in. Maintains constant tension automatically during tidal/current changes. ETO maintenance: Check motor IR, check brake condition (air gap of electromagnetic brake), check limit switches (inboard/outboard), check hydraulic pressure if hydraulic drive type, verify load cell calibration. Autotension interlock: Must be manually cancelled before departure — if left in auto, winch will keep paying out rope as ship moves away.

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?
oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. oral.text: Draw Torque speed diagram of induction motor.
oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kolkata surveyors, Sanjib — 'motor runs at slow speed after starting'
oral.answer: Definition: Motor runs stably at approximately 1/7th of synchronous speed instead of accelerating to full speed. Cause: 7th harmonic component in the air-gap flux creates a reluctance torque dip at 1/7 × Ns. Motor locks into this stable operating point instead of pulling through to full speed. Prevention: (1) Skew rotor slots — reduces harmonic content of air-gap flux. (2) Proper stator slot/rotor slot combination — avoid slot harmonics. (3) Chording of stator winding — reduces 5th and 7th harmonics. How to recognise: Motor starts, accelerates to ~1/7 speed, stops accelerating, runs noisily at low speed. Overcurrent relay may trip.

oral.answer: A transmitter-receiver pair that maintain exact angular correspondence. No power circuit — signal circuit only. Working: AC supply to transmitter rotor. Stator outputs 3-phase signal proportional to rotor angle. Receiver stator receives same 3-phase signal → receiver rotor aligns to same angle. Used on ships for: remote position indicators — rudder angle indicator, valve position indicator (remote), fuel tank level gauges, hatch cover position.

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib — 'Function of IGBT in cycloconverter'
oral.answer: Cycloconverter: Converts AC power directly to AC power at a DIFFERENT (lower) frequency — NO intermediate DC link. Limitation: Output frequency limited to <1/3 of input frequency. On 60Hz supply → max output 20Hz. On 50Hz → max 16.7Hz. Application: Large low-speed motors where low frequency needed (e.g. large propulsion drives, cement mills, rolling mills). IGBT in cycloconverter: IGBT (Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor) replaces SCR in modern designs. IGBT advantage: Gate-controlled turn-OFF (no natural commutation needed). Faster switching (2–20kHz vs 50–60Hz for SCR). Lower conduction losses. Better waveform quality. Dead ship context: After blackout, if cycloconverter-driven thruster — cannot start until ship's power restored fully.

oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?
oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. On ships, the power factor is almost always lagging because the predominant loads are induction motors (pumps, fans, compressors, cargo winch

oral.answer_heading: Turbocharger RPM Sensor — Type and Working
oral.answer: Type: Magnetic pickup (variable reluctance) sensor — most common. Some high-speed TCs use eddy current or optical sensors. Working: Ferromagnetic toothed wheel (phonic wheel) on TC shaft rotates past sensor tip. Each tooth passing changes magnetic flux through sensor coil — induces voltage pulse. Frequency of pulses = RPM of TC. Calibration: Count teeth × pulses per tooth × conversion factor = RPM. Usually preconfigured in tachometer. Faults: Oil on sensor tip → weak signal. Air gap too large (>2mm) → no signal. Broken tooth → erratic RPM. Cable fault → zero reading. Clean tip, check gap during maintenance.

oral.answer_heading: 4.1 Why Poor Power Factor is Harmful
oral.answer: A low power factor has significant negative consequences for the ship's electrical system and must be corrected. When PF is low (e.g., 0.6 lagging), a larger current must be drawn from the generator to supply the same useful KW of power. Additionally, generators must be rated at a higher KVA for the same useful KW output. oral.answer_heading: What is a UV Flame Detector?
oral.answer: A UV (ultraviolet) flame detector is a fire detector that senses the ultraviolet radiation emitted by flames. Unlike smoke detectors (which detect combustion products) or heat detectors (which detect temperature rise), the UV detector responds to the RADIATION emitted directly from the flame itself — giving an extremely fast response time (milliseconds). This makes it ideal for locations where a fire must be detected and suppressed before it spreads.

oral.answer_heading: 1.2 Two Methods of Cathodic Protection
oral.answer: Cathodic protection works by making the entire hull surface act as a cathode by supplying electrons externally, stopping the anodic dissolution reaction. There are two methods: sacrificial anode method (passive, galvanic) and impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP, active). Both methods force the hull potential to a negative value (typically –800 mV to –1050 mV relative to Ag/AgCl reference electrode) where steel corrosion effectively stops. The choice between methods depends on vessel size, dry dock interval, trade route, and maintenance capability.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Main Components of ICCP System
oral.answer: The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential. The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. oral.answer_heading: 1.1 What is Power Factor?
oral.answer: Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work. On ships, the power factor is almost always lagging because the predominant loads are induction motors (pumps, fans, compressors, cargo winch

oral.answer_heading: 1.1 RADAR — Working Principle
oral.answer: RADAR (Radio Detection And Ranging) detects objects by transmitting short pulses of high-frequency radio energy (microwave) from a rotating antenna and receiving the echoes reflected back from targets. The time taken for the pulse to travel to the target and return (two-way travel time, t) is used to calculate the range: Range = (c × t) / 2, where c = speed of light = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. The bearing of the target is determined by the orientation of the antenna at the moment of reception. The rotating antenna sweeps 360° continuously, building up a picture of all surrounding targets on the Plan Position Indicator (PPI) display. The minimum range of RADAR is limited by the pulse length — the transmitter must have finished transmitting before the echo arrives back, so very close targets cannot be detected during transmission. Two types of RADAR are fitted on ships as required by SOLAS: X-band RADA

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Vishwanathan — asked after navigation light questions
oral.answer: BITT = Built-In Integrity Test: Automatic self-test function built into the navigation light control panel. What it tests: Lamp filament continuity, supply fuse status, supply voltage level, cable continuity to each light fitting. How: Controller briefly energises each circuit and measures current — if current = 0 or below threshold → lamp/fuse fault → alarm generated. Alarm output: Audible + visual alarm on bridge panel. Alarm logged with timestamp and fault location. SOLAS requirement: Navigation light controllers with BITT function are required on vessels built after certain dates — exact date per Administration. ETO action on BITT alarm: Check lamp at fitting location. Replace lamp. Reset alarm. Test BITT — confirm clear.

oral.answer_heading: 2.1 What is GMDSS and Its Purpose
oral.answer: GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is an internationally agreed system using satellite and terrestrial radio communications to ensure that distress alerts and maritime safety information reach shore rescue co-ordination centres (RCCs) and nearby ships anywhere in the world. It is mandated by SOLAS Chapter IV for vessels on international voyages. GMDSS replaced the old Morse code distress system in 1999. The system is based on the concept of sea areas — the radio equipment required on a ship depends on which sea areas it operates in, because different equipment has different range capabilities. The four GMDSS sea areas are defined by the coverage of terrestrial VHF and MF/HF radio communications combined with satellite coverage. oral.answer_heading: What is WIDAS?
oral.answer: WIDAS = Water Ingress Detection and Alarm System. It is a monitoring system that detects the presence of water in enclosed spaces — cargo holds, void spaces, chain lockers, ballast tanks, fore and aft peaks — and raises an alarm on the bridge before flooding becomes structurally critical. WIDAS was introduced after a series of bulk carrier losses in the 1990s where water ingress in holds was not detected until too late.

oral.answer_heading: 3.2 SART — Search and Rescue Transponder
oral.answer: The SART (Search and Rescue Radar Transponder) is a survival craft locating device that operates at 9 GHz — the same frequency as X-band RADAR. It is a passive device carried on survival craft (lifeboats, liferafts) that remains silent until it receives a 9 GHz RADAR pulse from a searching vessel or aircraft. When triggered, it responds by transmitting a series of 12 pulses on the same frequency, creating a distinctive 12-dot line pattern on the searching vessel's X-band RADAR PPI display, extending radially from the SART's position. The SART can respond to a ship's RADAR at a range of approximately 5 nautical miles and to an aircraft's RADAR at approximately 10 nautical miles. oral.answer_heading: 2.1 What is GMDSS and Its Purpose
oral.answer: GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is an internationally agreed system using satellite and terrestrial radio communications to ensure that distress alerts and maritime safety information reach shore rescue co-ordination centres (RCCs) and nearby ships anywhere in the world. It is mandated by SOLAS Chapter IV for vessels on international voyages. GMDSS replaced the old Morse code distress system in 1999. The system is based on the concept of sea areas — the radio equipment required on a ship depends on which sea areas it operates in, because different equipment has different range capabilities. The four GMDSS sea areas are defined by the coverage of terrestrial VHF and MF/HF radio communications combined with satellite coverage. oral.answer_heading: 3.1 EPIRB — Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon
oral.answer: The EPIRB is a self-contained battery-powered radio transmitter that, when activated, transmits a coded distress signal on 406 MHz to the COSPAS-SARSAT network of polar-orbiting and geostationary satellites. The signal contains the ship's unique 15-digit hexadecimal identification code (registered to the vessel) and, if a GPS receiver is incorporated (GPS-EPIRB), the ship's precise position. The COSPAS-SARSAT satellites relay the distress signal to a Local User Terminal (LUT) on the ground, which computes or receives the position and forwards the alert to the Mission Control Centre (MCC) and then to the Rescue Co-ordination Centre (RCC) responsible for that area. The EPIRB also transmits on 121.5 MHz (homing frequency) — search and rescue aircraft and vessels use a 121.5 MHz receiver to home in on the EPIRB once in the general search area. oral.answer_heading: 2.1 Pressure Transducer — Working Principle
oral.answer: A pressure transducer converts fluid pressure into an electrical signal (typically 4–20 mA current loop or 0–10V DC). The sensing element is a strain gauge bonded to a diaphragm or a piezoelectric crystal, or a capacitance-based sensor. When pressure is applied to the diaphragm, it deflects slightly. Strain gauges bonded to the diaphragm measure the strain (deformation) — the resistance of the strain gauge changes proportionally to the strain (resistance increases when stretched, decreases when compressed). This resistance change is measured by a Wheatstone bridge circuit inside the transducer and converted to a 4–20 mA signal proportional to the pressure range. The 4 mA represents zero pressure (or minimum of range) and 20 mA represents the full-scale pressure. oral.answer_heading: What is PFOS?
oral.answer: PFOS = Perfluorooctane Sulfonate. A synthetic fluorochemical used in AFFF (Aqueous Film-Forming Foam) firefighting agents because of its exceptional ability to suppress flammable liquid fires by forming a thin aqueous film on the fuel surface. It was the standard foam type in engine rooms and pump rooms for decades. However, PFOS is a persistent organic pollutant (POP) — it accumulates in living organisms and the environment, causes cancer and reproductive harm, and does not break down naturally.

oral.answer: Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar. oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Wad — 'types of governors? which type on main engine?'
oral.answer: 1. MECHANICAL (Centrifugal / Flyball) governor: Rotating flyweights driven by engine. As speed increases → flyweights fly out → fuel rack reduces. Simple, robust, no external power. Used on older main engines and some AEs. 2. HYDRAULIC-MECHANICAL (Woodward type): Flyball + hydraulic servo amplifier. More precise than pure mechanical. Used on most diesel generators onboard. 3. ELECTRONIC (PID-based): Speed sensor (magnetic pickup) → electronic controller → actuator on fuel rack. Most precise. Used on modern DGs and electronically controlled main engines. Main engine governor type: Most 2-stroke slow-speed diesels use hydraulic-mechanical (Woodward) or electronic governor. Modern MAN B&W/Wartsila → electronic. Exam answer: 'DG typically uses hydraulic-mechanical Woodward governor. ME uses electronic governor on modern ships.'

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

oral.answer_heading: Battery maintenance procedure:
oral.answer: 1. MONTHLY CHECK: Verify trickle charger is connected and charging (charger indicator green). Measure battery terminal voltage — fully charged: 12.6–12.8V (12V system). Record. 2. oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. oral.text: PPE for ETO for working on HV and LV
oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
oral.answer: Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition. Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer. Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour. Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference. HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

OCR = fault protection (cables, busbar). Both may be present — different trip times. Fuse vs OCR: Fuse is sacrificial (single-use), trips on overcurrent, protects cables. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.

oral.answer_heading: When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
oral.answer: 1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up. 2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field. 3. True leakage current: Remains constant throughout. Flows through actual impurities/defects in insulation. At 1 minute: Absorption current still significant → reading appears lower than true insulation resistance. At 10 minutes: Absorption current largely decayed → reading approaches true leakage current only → accurate IR value. PI = R(10 min) / R(1 min). Good insulation: PI > 2.0. Questionable: 1.0–2.0. Dangerous: < 1.0 — do NOT energise. High PI = insulation polarises well = clean, dry, good quality. Low PI = insulation contaminated or deteriorated.

oral.answer: GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is an internationally agreed system using satellite and terrestrial radio communications to ensure that distress alerts and maritime safety information reach shore rescue co-ordination centres (RCCs) and nearby ships anywhere in the world. oral.answer: Class of fire: Class F — cooking oils and fats at high temperature (above their auto-ignition point ~340°C). Extinguisher: WET CHEMICAL extinguisher (potassium acetate/citrate solution). Creates a soapy layer (saponification) that seals the oil surface, cools the fire. Fixed system for galley: Wet chemical automatic suppression system (e.g. Ansul R-102, Amerex). Heat detector above cooking equipment activates system. Shuts down fuel/power to cooking equipment simultaneously.

oral.text: Battery capacity test..how to do and how frequently have to do.
oral.answer_heading: How battery capacity is measured:
oral.answer: Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time. Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable. Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature. Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."

oral.answer: 6. ACTIVATE CO₂ FIXED SYSTEM: For holds fitted with CO₂ — follow activation procedure. Verify hold is SEALED before flooding. CO₂ smothers fire by displacing oxygen. 7. If IG (inert gas) system available: Flood hold with inert gas — nitrogen or CO₂ blend. Maintain gas blanket. 8. After flooding: DO NOT OPEN HOLD for minimum 24 hours — CO₂ takes time to extinguish deep-seated fires in cargo. 9. Monitor hold temperature: Temperature probes in hold show whether fire is spreading (rising temp) or dying (falling temp).

oral.answer_heading: 🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Cross-questions after brushless alternator explanation
oral.answer: Rotating diode failure detection: stroboscope check during running — check for discoloured or pitted diodes. Also: unbalanced output voltage or ripple on output indicates a failed diode. Overvoltage protection on exciter output: Zener diode suppressor across diode bank — clamps transient voltages. Overcurrent protection on main field winding: included in AVR — limits excitation current to prevent winding overheating. Thermistor protection: embedded in stator winding — trips if temperature exceeds Class F limit (155°C). No slip rings — advantage: eliminates brush wear, arcing, and brush-dust contamination. Reduces maintenance significantly.
